Cleft
KLEFT
noun, adjective
From the Saxon cleofan, to split — the past participle of cleave in its dividing sense. A cleft is a split, fissure, or crack; as an adjective, divided. English confusingly holds two verbs cleave, one meaning to split apart and one to stick fast, and this word belongs to the first.

Biblical Definition

A cleft is a split, and Scripture uses it at three very different scales. In the law it is anatomical and defining: “every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat” (Deu 14:6). Two marks were required together, and the double test is instructive — the divided hoof, visible in the animal’s walk, and the chewing of the cud, its inward work. Neither alone sufficed; the camel chewed and did not divide, the swine divided and did not chew. In the prophets the scale is geological: “the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire” (Mic 1:4), the earth itself splitting at the approach of God. And in the clefts of the rocks men hide: “To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty” (Isa 2:21) — terror driving men into the stone. Yet the same clefts are a place of safety and of love: “O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance” (Son 2:14). Two men in a cleft of the same rock: one hiding from God’s face, one called to show his.

Webster 1828 Definition

A split, fissure, or crack; as an adjective, divided. Used of the parted hoof, of valleys split before God, and of the rock-clefts men hide in.

CLEFT, pp. of cleave; divided; split; parted asunder.

CLEFT, n. A space or opening made by splitting; a crevice; a fissure.

From the Saxon cleofan, to split, to divide.

To be distinguished from the other verb cleave, Saxon clifian, to adhere or stick fast.

Deu 14:6: the beast that cleaveth the cleft into two claws — the divided hoof.

Key Scripture

Deu 14:6 — "And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat."

Mic 1:4 — "And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place."

Isa 2:21 — "To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth."

Son 2:14 — "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely."

Modern Corruption

The clean-beast test required two marks together — the visible walk and the inward chewing — and every counterfeit of Christian profession fails by keeping one and dropping the other.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abiding use of the divided hoof is diagnostic. The law required two signs in the same animal: a parted hoof, which shows in how the creature walks and is visible to any observer, and the chewing of the cud, which is inward, slow, and repeated. The camel and the coney chewed but did not divide; the swine divided but did not chew. Neither was clean. Read as the older writers read it, this is a picture of profession and practice, of inward meditation and outward walk, and it exposes both counterfeits at once. There is the man whose conduct is faultless and whose inner life is empty of the word, and the man who ruminates endlessly on doctrine and whose walk is undivided from the world’s.

Recover the plain sense: neither mark alone was ever sufficient, and God appointed the double test because either can be counterfeited by itself. The cud is the man in Psa 1 whose delight is in the law of the LORD and who meditates in it day and night; the parted hoof is the same man who walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly. Then take the clefts as the gospel comfort behind the warning. Men will one day call on the rocks to hide them from the face of Him that sitteth on the throne, and the rocks will not help them; but the Bridegroom calls His dove out of the clefts to show her face, and Moses was hidden in a clift of the rock while the glory passed by. The rock is the same. What differs is whether one is hiding from God or hidden by Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon cleofan, to split — a fissure; the parted hoof, the split valleys, and the rock-cleft that hides or shelters.

expand to see more

Cleft — Saxon cleofan, to split; past participle of cleave (to divide).

Distinct from the other cleave (Saxon clifian), to stick fast.

Deu 14:6: the cleft hoof, one of two marks required together.

Mic 1:4: valleys cleft as wax before the fire at God’s approach.

Isa 2:21 and Son 2:14: the same rock-clefts hide the terrified and shelter the beloved.

Usage

"Two marks were required together; the camel chewed without dividing, the swine divided without chewing."

"The parted hoof is the visible walk; the cud is the inward meditation."

"Isa 2:21 hides men from God; Son 2:14 calls the beloved out of the same clefts."
